patient.chief_complaint: Campus police and EMS called after student found convulsing in dormitory hallway, 12 minutes duration
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. White is a 24-year-old college student with no prior epilepsy who is brought by campus EMS after being found convulsing in his dormitory hallway by a friend. The friend reports that the patient attended an off-campus party last night where he used MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine, ecstasy) approximately 8 hours prior to seizure onset. He appears to have developed a seizure while returning to his room. The friend estimated continuous seizure activity for approximately 12 minutes before EMS arrived. No prior seizures. He is on buspirone for anxiety which is relevant: buspirone lowers seizure threshold slightly. MDMA is a potent releaser of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. MDMA-related seizures can occur through multiple mechanisms: direct stimulant effect, hyponatremia from excessive water intake (MDMA causes SIADH and users are instructed to drink water - they often overdrink), hyperthermia, and serotonin syndrome. His temperature on arrival is 40.2°C — critical hyperthermia. The combination of MDMA, hyperthermia, hyponatremia, and buspirone (which also has serotonergic properties through partial 5-HT1A agonism) creates a complex clinical picture that must be urgently addressed. Hyperthermia >40°C in SE is a neurological emergency requiring active cooling.

output.summary: Rhabdomyolysis with AKI: CK above 10,000 U/L is associated with high risk for acute kidney injury. Aggressive IV isotonic saline targeting urine output 1–3 mL/kg/h is standard management. Hyperthermia is a potent driver of ongoing muscle breakdown; temperature management is integral to limiting CK rise. Hyperkalaemia from rhabdomyolysis requires cardiac monitoring; calcium gluconate and renal replacement therapy may be required in severe cases.

results.finding: Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome: clonus (spontaneous, inducible, or ocular) + agitation/confusion + hyperthermia + diaphoresis + diarrhea
Hunter criteria positive when clonus (spontaneous, inducible, or ocular) is present together with hyperthermia and at least one other feature (agitation, diaphoresis, or diarrhea)
Buspirone (5-HT1A partial agonist) + MDMA (serotonin release) = serotonin syndrome risk
Treatment: benzodiazepines, active cooling, cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) oral/NG 12 mg loading + 2 mg q2h
Avoid non-selective MAOIs and other serotonergic agents during acute phase

output.summary: Serotonin syndrome — Hunter criteria require clonus plus at least one additional serotonergic feature. MDMA combined with serotonergic agents (e.g. buspirone) increases serotonin syndrome risk. Standard management includes benzodiazepines, active cooling, and cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) 12 mg loading dose oral or nasogastric, then 2 mg every 2 h. Serotonergic agents should be withheld during the acute phase.
